title: HTTP, TLS & Connections
subtitle: Load the same 31-file page over HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 and watch round trips and blocking change the clock.
learn: Why a new connection costs round trips, and what TLS 1.3 saves
How keep-alive and connection pools avoid repeating that cost
What head-of-line blocking is, at the HTTP layer and at the TCP layer
How HTTP/2 multiplexing and HTTP/3 over QUIC each remove one kind of blocking

steps.title: 31 files, one slow wire
steps.body: A page needs one HTML file plus 30 small assets (CSS, scripts, images). The user is 50 ms away by round trip (RTT: a message out and its reply back). We ignore download time, so only round trips and waiting count. The question: how should the browser and server talk so all 31 requests finish fast? HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 each answer differently, and the numbers show why.
steps.idea: With many small files, the cost is mostly round trips, not bandwidth.
steps.caption: One browser, one edge proxy, 31 resources to fetch.

steps.title: A new connection is not free
steps.body: Before any HTTP data moves, the browser opens a TCP connection. TCP is the layer that delivers bytes reliably. Its handshake is SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK ('hello', 'hello back', 'ready') and costs one round trip. Then TLS adds encryption. With TLS 1.3 that is one more round trip, so the first request cannot leave until about 100 ms have passed. Older TLS 1.2 needed two round trips for TLS, making it 150 ms. This step animates the TCP half. TLS comes next.
steps.idea: TCP plus TLS 1.3 costs 2 round trips before the first request. TLS 1.2 costs 3.
steps.caption: TCP handshake: round trip 1 of 2 (TLS is next).

steps.title: Inside the TLS 1.3 handshake
steps.body: In TLS 1.3 the client's first message already carries its half of a key exchange. The server replies with its half, its certificate and a Finished message, and both sides can now work out the same secret keys. The certificate proves the server owns the domain, so you are not talking to an impostor. The client then sends its own Finished together with the first HTTP request. On a repeat visit, a resumption ticket can allow 0-RTT (data sent in the very first message). An attacker can replay that data, so use it only for idempotent requests, ones that are harmless to repeat, like GET.
steps.idea: TLS 1.3 needs one round trip. Resumption can skip it, but only for replay-safe requests.
steps.caption: Keys agreed in a single round trip.

steps.title: HTTP/1.1 reuses the connection
steps.body: HTTP/1.1 keeps the TCP connection open after a response (keep-alive), so later requests skip the handshakes. But one connection carries one request at a time: the next request waits for the previous response. With 31 requests of 50 ms each on one connection, the page needs 100 ms of setup plus 31 × 50 ms, about 1,650 ms. The animation shows requests going out one after another.
steps.idea: Keep-alive removes repeated handshakes, but HTTP/1.1 still handles one request per connection at a time.
steps.caption: 31 requests queue one after another on one connection.

steps.title: Head-of-line blocking and the six-connection hack
steps.body: Head-of-line blocking means one slow item holds up everything queued behind it, like one slow person at the front of a single checkout line. On an HTTP/1.1 connection, a 2-second API call stalls every request after it, because responses must come back in order. Browsers work around this by opening about six connections per host. Time: 100 ms setup, 50 ms for the HTML, then 30 assets in 5 rounds of 6 (250 ms), so about 400 ms, assuming the extra connections open early. The price is six handshakes and six sets of server memory.
steps.idea: HTTP/1.1 fights head-of-line blocking by multiplying connections, which is costly.
steps.caption: Six connections share the 31 requests.

steps.title: Pools behind the proxy
steps.body: The same idea applies behind the proxy. The edge proxy keeps a pool of connections to the app server and the auth service that are already open and encrypted. It borrows one for each request instead of dialing a new one. Inside a data center a round trip is only about 0.5 ms, so a new handshake costs roughly 1 ms plus CPU for the cryptography. At thousands of requests per second that still adds up and can exhaust ports. Give pools a size limit and an idle timeout shorter than the server's, or you may send requests on connections the server already closed.
steps.idea: A connection pool pays the setup cost once and shares it. Size it and expire it deliberately.
steps.caption: The proxy reuses warm connections to its backends.

steps.title: HTTP/2 multiplexes streams
steps.body: HTTP/2 splits traffic into small frames, each tagged with a stream ID, so many requests and responses interleave on one TCP connection. The browser sends all 30 asset requests at once instead of waiting in line. Time: 100 ms setup, 50 ms for the HTML, 50 ms for the burst of assets, about 200 ms. It uses a single connection and compresses headers. This fixes head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer.
steps.idea: Multiplexing lets one connection carry many independent requests at the same time.
steps.caption: 31 streams interleave on one connection.

steps.title: One lost packet stalls every stream
steps.body: HTTP/2 still rides on TCP, which delivers bytes strictly in order. If one packet is lost, TCP holds back everything after it, even frames of unaffected streams, until the retransmission (a resend) arrives. On clean wired networks this is rare. On lossy mobile links with 1 to 2 percent loss it happens often, and HTTP/2 can lose most of its advantage. Six separate HTTP/1.1 connections suffer less, because a drop stalls only the connection it hit. The 250 ms shown is a single-loss example (200 + 50 for one extra round trip). More losses add more.
steps.idea: HTTP/2 removes blocking in HTTP, but TCP's in-order delivery brings it back at the transport layer.
steps.caption: One dropped packet freezes every stream on the connection.

steps.title: HTTP/3 and QUIC
steps.body: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which is built on UDP (a bare-bones transport with no ordering or retransmission of its own). QUIC adds reliability, encryption and streams itself. Its transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes are combined, so setup takes 1 round trip instead of 2. Each stream recovers losses on its own, so a lost packet delays only the streams whose data it carried. Time: 50 ms setup + 50 ms HTML + 50 ms assets = 150 ms. A first visit usually starts on TCP and learns about HTTP/3 from an Alt-Svc header. Browsers fall back to TCP if UDP is blocked.
steps.idea: QUIC cuts setup to 1 round trip and gives each stream its own loss recovery.
steps.caption: One-round-trip setup. Each stream recovers from loss separately.

steps.title: Fewer round trips, less blocking
steps.body: Every new connection costs round trips, so reuse them: keep-alive for clients, pools behind the proxy. HTTP/1.1 sends one request at a time per connection. HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection. HTTP/3 uses QUIC to remove blocking at the TCP level too. TLS 1.3 is the modern default (and required by HTTP/3). The numbers are idealized, but on healthy networks the ordering usually holds.
steps.idea: Reuse connections, multiplex requests, and avoid one in-order pipe shared by unrelated streams.
steps.caption: Same page: HTTP/1.1 1650 ms (400 with 6 connections), HTTP/2 200 ms, HTTP/3 150 ms.

quiz.q: A server is 40 ms away (round trip). How long before the first HTTP request can be sent on a brand-new TCP + TLS 1.3 connection?
options: About 40 ms
About 80 ms
About 120 ms
About 160 ms
quiz.why: TCP needs one round trip and TLS 1.3 needs one more, so 2 x 40 ms = 80 ms. TLS 1.2 would add a third round trip.

quiz.q: Why does HTTP/1.1 keep-alive alone not make a 30-asset page fast?
options: Keep-alive only works for HTML
Keep-alive disables encryption
The server closes the connection after each response
Each connection still handles one request at a time, so requests queue
quiz.why: Keep-alive removes repeated handshakes, but responses on a connection come back in order, so requests wait on each other.

quiz.q: On a lossy mobile network, one packet is dropped during an HTTP/2 page load. What happens?
options: Only the stream owning that packet waits
HTTP/2 automatically opens a second connection
All streams on the TCP connection stall until the retransmission arrives
The browser switches to HTTP/1.1 immediately
quiz.why: TCP delivers bytes in order, so a gap blocks everything behind it, including unrelated streams. QUIC avoids this with per-stream recovery.

quiz.q: Your proxy sometimes fails requests with 'connection reset' right after sitting idle. The app server closes idle connections after 60 s. What is the best fix?
options: Set the proxy's pool idle timeout below 60 s
Disable the connection pool
Switch the proxy to HTTP/1.0
Raise the app server's timeout to 24 hours
quiz.why: If the proxy holds a pooled connection longer than the server does, it can send on a connection already closed. Expiring idle connections first avoids that race.

quiz.q: Which statement about HTTP/3 is correct?
options: It runs over TCP with a faster handshake
It runs over QUIC on UDP and recovers lost packets per stream
It removes the need for TLS
It requires one connection per request
quiz.why: HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP, with TLS 1.3 built in and independent loss recovery per stream.

cheatsheet.def: TCP 1 RTT + TLS 1.3 1 RTT = 2 RTTs before the first request. TLS 1.2 adds a third. QUIC combines both into 1 RTT.
Leaving a connection open for more requests, so later ones skip TCP and TLS setup. Default in HTTP/1.1.
A slow or lost item delays everything queued behind it. It occurs at the HTTP layer (1.1) and the TCP layer (2).
Many request/response streams interleaved as frames on one TCP connection, with header compression (HPACK).
HTTP over UDP-based QUIC: built-in TLS 1.3, per-stream loss recovery, connection IDs that survive network changes.
A set of warm connections reused across requests. Tune max size and set idle timeout below the peer's timeout.
Sending data in the first flight on a repeat visit. Replayable by attackers, so use only for idempotent requests.
Header (or DNS HTTPS record) telling clients that HTTP/3 is available; clients fall back to TCP if UDP fails.
